Physiology 05.question: ১) Which is a part of telencephalon?
Physiology 05.exp:
The telencephalon is the most rostral part of the forebrain and develops mainly into the cerebral hemispheres, including the cerebral cortex, underlying white matter, and basal nuclei.

Other options:

  • Thalamus: Part of the diencephalon.

  • Hypothalamus: Also part of the diencephalon.

  • Pons: Part of the brainstem, specifically the metencephalon.

High-yield Neuroanatomy recall:
Telencephalon → cerebral cortex + cerebral white matter + basal nuclei

Exam pearl:
Cerebral cortex = telencephalon; thalamus & hypothalamus = diencephalon.

Physiology 05.question: ২) Neurons have all of the following special properties except......?
Physiology 05.exp:
Most mature neurons are highly differentiated and do not normally undergo cell division or replication. They are considered post-mitotic cells. Therefore, replicating is not a characteristic property of mature neurons.

Neurons are primarily characterized by excitability and the ability to conduct electrical impulses.

Other options:

  • Excitable: Correct. Neurons respond to appropriate stimuli by generating action potentials.

  • Non-dividing: Correct for most mature neurons.

  • Non-replicating: Correct for most mature neurons.

High-yield Neuroanatomy recall:
Mature neuron → excitable + conductive + generally non-dividing/non-replicating.

Physiology 05.question: ৩) Which function is maintained at spinal cord level?
Physiology 05.exp:
The spinal cord can maintain certain autonomic reflex functions independently of higher brain centers. Urinary bladder emptying (micturition) is controlled by a spinal reflex center mainly located in the sacral spinal cord (S2–S4), although normal voluntary control requires higher centers.

Other options:

  • Memory storage: Mainly involves the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.

  • Equilibrium control: Mainly coordinated by the vestibular system and cerebellum.

  • Respiration control: Primarily controlled by respiratory centers in the medulla and pons.

High-yield Spinal cord recall:
S2–S4 → parasympathetic micturition center → bladder contraction and urination.

Exam pearl:
Micturition is a spinal reflex, but higher centers normally control and modify it.

Physiology 05.question: ৪) Which is a class-1 neurotransmitter?
Physiology 05.exp:
In the commonly used classification of neurotransmitters:

Class I neurotransmitters = small-molecule, rapidly acting transmitters, which include acetylcholine and the amino acids.

Therefore, acetylcholine is a Class I neurotransmitter.

Other options:

  • Dopamine: A biogenic amine/catecholamine neurotransmitter, classified separately from Class I in this scheme.

  • GABA: An amino-acid neurotransmitter and often grouped with Class I small-molecule transmitters, so some textbooks may classify it differently depending on the classification system.

  • Nitric oxide: A gaseous neurotransmitter/neuromodulator, synthesized on demand rather than stored in vesicles.

High-yield Neurotransmitter recall:
A common physiological classification is:

  • Small-molecule transmitters: ACh, amino acids, biogenic amines

  • Neuropeptides

  • Other unconventional transmitters: NO, etc.

Exam pearl:
For this MCQ, the expected answer is acetylcholine.

Physiology 05.question: ৫) Which is the longest tract of the nervous system?
Physiology 05.exp:
The corticospinal tract is considered the longest descending tract of the nervous system. It originates mainly from the cerebral cortex and descends through the brainstem and spinal cord to influence motor neurons at various spinal levels.

Other options:

  • Tract of Goll (fasciculus gracilis): Ascending dorsal column tract carrying fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the lower body.

  • Tract of Burdach (fasciculus cuneatus): Ascending dorsal column tract carrying similar sensations from the upper body.

  • Spinothalamic tract: Ascending tract carrying pain, temperature, and crude touch.

High-yield Neuroanatomy recall:
Corticospinal tract → longest major descending motor tract.

Exam pearl:
Longest tract → corticospinal tract.

Physiology 05.question: ৬) Which is not a feature of extrapyramidal tract lesion?
Physiology 05.exp:
There is an important terminology issue here. Spastic paralysis, exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, and clonus are characteristic of an upper motor neuron (UMN)/pyramidal tract lesion, rather than a typical extrapyramidal lesion.

However, clasp-knife phenomenon is also a feature of spasticity, classically associated with pyramidal/UMN lesions. Therefore, saying “clasp knife reaction absent” is not a reliable statement for a classic UMN lesion.

For the given options, the expected exam answer is “clasp knife reaction absent”, because the question is apparently contrasting extrapyramidal features with pyramidal/UMN signs.

Other options:

  • Spastic paralysis: More characteristic of pyramidal (corticospinal) tract lesions.

  • Exaggerated deep reflexes: Typical of UMN/pyramidal lesions.

  • Clonus may be present: Also a classic UMN/pyramidal sign.

  • Clasp-knife reaction absent: Expected as the “not a feature” answer in this question.

High-yield Neuroanatomy recall:
Pyramidal/UMN lesion → spasticity + hyperreflexia + clonus + Babinski + clasp-knife phenomenon.

Exam pearl:
Clasp-knife, clonus, hyperreflexia, and spasticity = UMN/pyramidal signs.

Physiology 05.question: ৭) Anterior spinothalamic tract carries sensation for...?
Physiology 05.exp:
The anterior spinothalamic tract carries crude touch and pressure sensations from the body to the thalamus.

Other options:

  • Pain: Mainly carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract.

  • Temperature: Mainly carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract.

  • Vibration: Carried by the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway.

High-yield Spinothalamic recall:

  • Anterior spinothalamic → crude touch + pressure

  • Lateral spinothalamic → pain + temperature

  • Dorsal column → fine touch + vibration + proprioception

Exam pearl:
Anterior = crude touch; lateral = pain & temperature.

Physiology 05.question: ৮) Fast pain is carried by which type of nerve fiber?
Physiology 05.exp:
Explanation:
Fast pain is carried by thinly myelinated Aδ fibers. They conduct impulses relatively rapidly and produce sharp, pricking, well-localized pain.

Other options:

  • Aα fibers: Mainly carry proprioceptive and motor-related information; not pain fibers.

  • Aβ fibers: Carry touch, pressure, and vibration.

  • C fibers: Carry slow, dull, burning, poorly localized pain; they are unmyelinated and conduct slowly.

High-yield Pain fiber recall:

  • Aδ → fast pain → sharp/pricking

  • C → slow pain → dull/burning/aching

Exam pearl:
Fast pain = Aδ; slow pain = C fibers.

Physiology 05.question: ৯) Which is not a feature of referred pain ?
Physiology 05.exp:
Referred pain is pain perceived at a site different from its actual origin, commonly from a visceral structure and felt in a somatic area sharing the same spinal segments. It is typically diffuse and poorly localized, rather than highly localized.

Other options:

  • ক) Originated from viscera: Correct feature of referred pain.

  • খ) Felt in other somatic areas: Correct; visceral pain may be perceived in a somatic region.

  • গ) Conducted by C fiber: Correct; visceral pain is predominantly carried by slow, unmyelinated C fibers.

High-yield Referred pain recall:
Visceral pain → poorly localized → often referred to a somatic area supplied by the same spinal segment.

Exam pearl:
Referred pain is poorly localized, not highly localized.

Physiology 05.question: ১০) The part of cell body from which axon arises is called....?
Physiology 05.exp:
The axon hillock is the specialized region of the neuronal cell body from which the axon arises. It is also the site where action potentials are typically initiated because it has a high density of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels.

Other options:

  • খ) Node of Ranvier: Gaps between myelin sheaths along a myelinated axon; important for saltatory conduction.

  • গ) Boutons terminaux: Terminal endings of an axon that contain synaptic vesicles and release neurotransmitters.

  • ঘ) Synaptic cleft: The microscopic gap between presynaptic and postsynaptic cells.

High-yield Neuroanatomy recall:
Cell body → axon hillock → axon → terminal boutons → synapse.

Exam pearl:
Axon arises from the axon hillock.

Physiology 05.question: ১১) Which order of sensory neuron carry sensation from spinal cord to thalamus ?
Physiology 05.exp:
The 2nd-order sensory neuron carries sensory information from the spinal cord (or brainstem) to the thalamus. It usually crosses over (decussates) before ascending to the thalamus.

The 1st-order neuron carries sensation from the peripheral receptor to the spinal cord/brainstem, while the 3rd-order neuron carries information from the thalamus to the cerebral cortex.

Other options:

  • ক) 1st: Receptor → spinal cord/brainstem.

  • গ) 3rd: Thalamus → sensory cortex.

  • ঘ) 4th: Not part of the standard 3-neuron sensory pathway.

High-yield Sensory pathway recall:
1st-order: Receptor → spinal cord/brainstem
2nd-order: Spinal cord/brainstem → thalamus
3rd-order: Thalamus → cerebral cortex

Exam pearl:
Spinal cord → thalamus = 2nd-order sensory neuron.

Physiology 05.question: ১২) Which glial cell causes myelination of CNS ?
Physiology 05.exp:
Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating glial cells of the CNS (brain and spinal cord). One oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of multiple axons.

Other options:

  • ক) Astrocytes: Provide structural and metabolic support and help maintain the blood–brain barrier; they do not form myelin.

  • গ) Schwann cells: Form myelin in the PNS, not CNS.

  • ঘ) Ependyma: Lines the ventricles of the brain and central canal of the spinal cord and is associated with CSF circulation.

High-yield Glial cell recall:
CNS myelin → Oligodendrocyte
PNS myelin → Schwann cell

Exam pearl:
Oligodendrocyte = CNS; Schwann cell = PNS.

Physiology 05.question: ১৩) Which is a feature of LMN lesion?
Physiology 05.exp:
A lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion damages the motor neuron or its axon, resulting in hyporeflexia or areflexia. Other typical features include flaccid paralysis, muscle wasting, fasciculations, and hypotonia.

Other options:

  • ক) Spastic paralysis: Feature of an UMN lesion.

  • গ) Babinski sign positive: Typically indicates an UMN lesion.

  • ঘ) Clonus present: Characteristic of UMN lesions due to hyperreflexia.

High-yield LMN vs UMN recall:
LMN: Flaccidity + wasting + fasciculations + ↓ reflexes
UMN: Spasticity + hyperreflexia + Babinski + clonus

Exam pearl:
LMN lesion → loss of the reflex arc → diminished/absent deep tendon reflexes.

Physiology 05.question: ১৪) Paralysis of both lower limb is called....?
Physiology 05.exp:
Paraplegia is paralysis affecting both lower limbs, usually due to a lesion involving the spinal cord or other motor pathways supplying the legs.

Other options:

  • ক) Hemiplegia: Paralysis of one side of the body (arm and leg).

  • খ) Diplegia: Paralysis affecting corresponding parts on both sides, classically both lower limbs more severely than upper limbs, especially in cerebral palsy.

  • ঘ) Quadriplegia: Paralysis of both upper and both lower limbs.

High-yield Neurology recall:

  • Hemiplegia → one side

  • Paraplegia → both lower limbs

  • Quadriplegia/Tetraplegia → all four limbs

Exam pearl:
Both lower limbs paralyzed = Paraplegia.

Physiology 05.question: ১৫) Which one is polysynaptic reflex arc?
Physiology 05.exp:
The withdrawal (flexor) reflex is a polysynaptic reflex because it involves one or more interneurons between the sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) neurons. It protects the body by rapidly withdrawing a limb from a painful stimulus

Other options:

  • ক) Stretch reflex: Monosynaptic; e.g., knee jerk reflex.

  • খ) Extension reflex: Generally refers to reflex extension and may involve interneuronal pathways, but it is not the classic answer for this MCQ.

  • গ) Crossed extension reflex: Polysynaptic, but it accompanies the withdrawal reflex and is classically considered a more complex associated reflex.

High-yield Reflex recall:
Stretch reflex → monosynaptic
Withdrawal reflex → polysynaptic

Exam pearl:
Painful stimulus → withdrawal reflex → polysynaptic.

Physiology 05.question: ১৬) Which one is a superficial reflex?
Physiology 05.exp:
The cremasteric reflex is a superficial cutaneous reflex. Stroking the medial aspect of the upper thigh causes elevation of the ipsilateral testis due to contraction of the cremaster muscle.

Other options:

  • ক) Vomiting reflex: A visceral/autonomic reflex.

  • খ) Light reflex: A cranial autonomic reflex involving the pupillary sphincter.

  • ঘ) Jaw jerk: A deep tendon (stretch) reflex, mediated mainly by CN V.

High-yield Reflex recall:
Common superficial reflexes include:

  • Abdominal reflex

  • Cremasteric reflex

  • Plantar reflex

  • Anal reflex

Exam pearl:
Cremasteric reflex = superficial reflex; afferent and efferent limbs are mainly via L1–L2.

Physiology 05.question: ১৭) Which one is a pathological reflex?
Physiology 05.exp:
The Babinski sign is a pathological reflex in adults. Stroking the lateral aspect of the sole normally produces plantar flexion of the toes. An extensor plantar response (dorsiflexion of the great toe with fanning of the other toes) suggests an upper motor neuron/corticospinal tract lesion.

Other options:

  • ক) Pupillary reflex: A normal physiological reflex.

  • গ) Corneal reflex: A normal superficial protective reflex mediated mainly by CN V and VII.

  • ঘ) Plantar reflex: A normal superficial reflex; the extensor response (Babinski sign) is pathological in adults.

High-yield Reflex recall:
Babinski positive → UMN/corticospinal tract lesion.
It can be physiological in infants because corticospinal tract myelination is incomplete.

Exam pearl:
Extensor plantar response in an adult = Babinski sign = UMN lesion.

Physiology 05.question: ১৮) Which is not a cause of hyperreflexia?
Physiology 05.exp:
LMN lesions (LMNL) cause hyporeflexia or areflexia, not hyperreflexia, because the reflex arc is disrupted. In contrast, UMN lesions, thyrotoxicosis, and tetanus can produce exaggerated reflexes.

Other options:

  • ক) UMNL: Causes hyperreflexia due to loss of descending inhibitory control.

  • গ) Thyrotoxicosis: Can cause brisk/exaggerated deep tendon reflexes.

  • ঘ) Tetanus: Causes generalized muscle rigidity and increased reflex activity.

High-yield Reflex recall:
UMN → hyperreflexia
LMN → hypo/areflexia

Exam pearl:
Hyperreflexia = think UMN; hyporeflexia = think LMN.

Physiology 05.question: ১৯) Which reflex causes flexion of forearm?
Physiology 05.exp:
The biceps jerk (biceps reflex) causes flexion of the forearm at the elbow due to contraction of the biceps brachii muscle. It is a deep tendon reflex mediated mainly by C5–C6 spinal segments, predominantly C5.

Other options:

  •  Triceps jerk: Causes extension of the forearm at the elbow; mainly C7–C8.

  •  Supinator jerk (brachioradialis reflex): Produces flexion of the elbow with some supination; mainly C5–C6.

  •  Pronator jerk: Produces pronation of the forearm.

High-yield Reflex recall:

  • Biceps jerk → elbow flexion → C5–C6

  • Triceps jerk → elbow extension → C7–C8

  • Supinator/brachioradialis jerk → elbow flexion/supination → C5–C6

Exam pearl:
Biceps reflex = elbow flexion = C5–C6.

Physiology 05.question: ২০) Which part of cerebellum controls planning and programming?
Physiology 05.exp:
The neocerebellum (cerebrocerebellum) is mainly concerned with planning, programming, initiation, and coordination of skilled voluntary movements. It receives major input from the cerebral cortex via the pontine nuclei and communicates with the motor cortex through the dentate nucleus and thalamus.

  • Archicerebellum (vestibulocerebellum): Balance and eye movements

  • Spinocerebellum: Posture, muscle tone, and ongoing coordination of movements

  • Neocerebellum: Planning and programming of skilled voluntary movements

High-yield Cerebellum recall:
Neocerebellum → planning & programming
Spinocerebellum → execution/coordination
Vestibulocerebellum → balance & eye movements

Exam pearl:
“Neo plans, Spino executes, Vestibulo balances.”

Physiology 05.question: ২১) 4th ventricle lies within......?
Physiology 05.exp:
The 4th ventricle is located in the hindbrain, specifically between the pons and medulla anteriorly and the cerebellum posteriorly. Embryologically, it develops from the metencephalon and myelencephalon.

  • 3rd ventricle → Diencephalon

  • Cerebral aqueduct → Midbrain

  • 4th ventricle → Hindbrain

  • Lateral ventricles → Cerebral hemispheres

High-yield Ventricular system recall:
Lateral ventricles → Telencephalon
3rd ventricle → Diencephalon
4th ventricle → Metencephalon + Myelencephalon

Exam pearl:
4th ventricle lies between the brainstem and cerebellum and belongs to the hindbrain.

Physiology 05.question: ২২) Xanthochromia of CSF is commonly seen in....?
Physiology 05.exp:
Xanthochromia refers to yellowish discoloration of CSF caused by the breakdown of hemoglobin into pigments such as bilirubin. It is classically seen in subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), usually becoming detectable several hours after the hemorrhage.

  • SAH: Xanthochromia is a classic finding.

  • Meningitis: CSF may be turbid with elevated WBCs and protein, but xanthochromia is not the characteristic finding.

  • GBS: Classically causes albuminocytologic dissociation—high protein with normal cell count.

High-yield CSF recall:
SAH → Xanthochromia
GBS → Albuminocytologic dissociation
Bacterial meningitis → Neutrophils + high protein + low glucose

Exam pearl:
Xanthochromic CSF = think SAH first.

Physiology 05.question: ২৩) Which is not a deep cerebellar nuclei?
Physiology 05.exp:
The deep cerebellar nuclei are four paired nuclei embedded within the cerebellar white matter:

  1. Dentate

  2. Emboliform

  3. Globose

  4. Fastigial

Stellate cells are cerebellar cortical interneurons, not a deep cerebellar nucleus.

High-yield Cerebellar nuclei recall:
“Don’t Eat Greasy Food” → Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial

Exam pearl:
Deep cerebellar nuclei = Dentate + Emboliform + Globose + Fastigial; Stellate is a cortical interneuron.

Physiology 05.question: ২৪) Inability to perform rapidly alternating movement is called...?
Physiology 05.exp:
Dysdiadochokinesia is the inability to perform rapid, alternating movements, such as rapidly pronating and supinating the forearm. It is a classic sign of cerebellar dysfunction.

  • Dysarthria: Difficulty in articulation of speech.

  • Past pointing: Overshooting or undershooting a target due to impaired coordination.

  • Dysmetria: Inability to accurately control the range, force, and distance of a movement.

  • Dysdiadochokinesia: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements.

High-yield Cerebellar signs recall:
Dysdiadochokinesia → rapid alternating movements
Dysmetria → inaccurate distance/range of movement
Past pointing → overshooting/undershooting target
Intention tremor → tremor increases during purposeful movement

Exam pearl:
“Rapid alternating movement impaired = Dysdiadochokinesia.”

Physiology 05.question: ২৫) Which acts as final relay station for sensory stimuli?
Physiology 05.exp:
The thalamus acts as the major relay station for sensory information to the cerebral cortex. Almost all sensory pathways, except olfaction, relay through the thalamus before reaching the cortex.

  • Thalamus → major sensory relay to cerebral cortex

  • Hypothalamus → autonomic, endocrine, and homeostatic regulation

  • Basal ganglia → motor control

  • Internal capsule → major white-matter pathway carrying ascending and descending fibers

High-yield Thalamus recall:
All major sensory modalities except smell → thalamus → cerebral cortex.

Exam pearl:
“Thalamus = gateway/relay station to the cortex; smell is the exception.”

Physiology 05.question: ২৬) Which acts as biological clock of the body?
Physiology 05.exp:
The hypothalamus, particularly the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), acts as the body's biological clock. The SCN receives light-related information from the retina and regulates the circadian rhythm, including the sleep–wake cycle and hormonal rhythms.

High-yield Hypothalamus recall:
Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) → master circadian clock
Pineal gland → melatonin secretion, regulated by the SCN.

Exam pearl:
“Biological clock = Suprachiasmatic nucleus of hypothalamus.”

Physiology 05.question: ২৭) The urge, initiative & drive to act arising from inside oneself is called....?
Physiology 05.exp:
Conation refers to the mental faculty concerned with will, intention, motivation, and purposeful action—the urge or drive to initiate and perform an activity.

The three traditional components of mental activity are:

  • Cognition → Knowing/thinking

  • Affection → Feeling/emotion

  • Conation → Willing/acting

High-yield Psychiatry recall:
Cognition = knowing
Affection = feeling
Conation = willing/doing

Exam pearl:
“Cognition knows, affection feels, conation acts.”

Physiology 05.question: ২৮) Which part of limbic system is concerned with converting recent memory to long term memory?
Physiology 05.exp:
The hippocampus is essential for consolidation of recent/short-term memories into long-term memory. Damage to the hippocampus causes anterograde amnesia, with impaired ability to form new long-term memories.

  • Hippocampus → memory consolidation

  • Amygdala → emotion, especially fear and emotional memory

  • Cingulate gyrus → emotion, motivation, and limbic processing

  • Parahippocampal gyrus → memory-related processing and contextual information

High-yield Limbic system recall:
Hippocampus → consolidation of new memories
Amygdala → emotional memory/fear
Mammillary bodies → memory circuit (Papez circuit)

Exam pearl:
“Hippocampus converts recent memories into long-term memories.”

Physiology 05.question: ২৯) Which is known as sympathetic outflow?
Physiology 05.exp:
The sympathetic nervous system is called the thoracolumbar outflow because its preganglionic neurons arise from the intermediolateral cell column of spinal cord segments T1–L2.

In contrast, the parasympathetic nervous system has a craniosacral outflow, arising from the brainstem and sacral spinal cord (S2–S4).

High-yield Autonomic nervous system recall:
Sympathetic → Thoracolumbar → T1–L2
Parasympathetic → Craniosacral → Brainstem + S2–S4

Exam pearl:
“Sympathetic = Thoracolumbar; Parasympathetic = Craniosacral.”

Physiology 05.question: ৩০) Which neurotransmitter seems to be associated with production of sleep?
Physiology 05.exp:
Serotonin (5-HT) is involved in the regulation of the sleep–wake cycle and is associated with the promotion and regulation of sleep. Serotonergic neurons in the raphe nuclei of the brainstem contribute to sleep regulation and also serve as precursors for melatonin synthesis indirectly.

  • Serotonin → sleep regulation

  • GABA → major inhibitory neurotransmitter; promotes sleep by reducing neuronal activity

  • Glutamate → major excitatory neurotransmitter

  • Acetylcholine → promotes cortical activation and REM sleep

High-yield Sleep neurotransmitter recall:
Serotonin → sleep regulation
GABA → sleep-promoting inhibition
Acetylcholine → REM sleep/cortical activation
Glutamate → excitatory neurotransmission

Exam pearl:
For classic MCQs, “neurotransmitter associated with production of sleep” = Serotonin.

Physiology 05.question: ৩১) Severe increase of protein in CSF is the feature of.....
Physiology 05.exp:
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) classically produces albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF—markedly increased protein with a normal or near-normal WBC count. This occurs due to inflammation of the spinal nerve roots.

  • GBS → markedly ↑ CSF protein + normal cell count

  • Meningitis → ↑ WBCs + ↑ protein; glucose may be reduced

  • SAH → xanthochromia + increased RBCs/protein

  • ICSOL → CSF findings are variable and not characterized by severe protein elevation

High-yield GBS recall:
Albuminocytologic dissociation = ↑ protein with normal cell count.

Exam pearl:
“Very high CSF protein without pleocytosis → think GBS.”

Physiology 05.question: ৩২) Elevated ICP is defined when it is more than or equal to....... mmHg for more than...... minutes?
Physiology 05.exp:
Intracranial pressure (ICP) is considered elevated when it is ≥20 mmHg for more than 5 minutes, particularly in the context of severe traumatic brain injury (TBI). Sustained intracranial hypertension can reduce cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) and cause cerebral ischemia.

High-yield ICP recall:

  • Normal adult ICP: approximately 5–15 mmHg

  • ICP ≥20 mmHg sustained for >5 minutes → intracranial hypertension

  • CPP = MAP − ICP

Exam pearl:
“20 for 5 = raised ICP.”

Physiology 05.question: ৩৩) Parkinsonism is a disease of which part of brain?
Physiology 05.exp:
Parkinsonism results primarily from dysfunction of the basal ganglia, especially degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. This causes reduced dopamine input to the striatum, leading to impaired regulation of voluntary movement.

Classical features include bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and postural instability.

High-yield Basal ganglia recall:
Parkinson disease → substantia nigra pars compacta degeneration → ↓ dopamine → basal ganglia dysfunction.

Exam pearl:
“Parkinson = loss of dopamine from substantia nigra.”

Physiology 05.question: ৩৪) How many primary sensations of taste are there?
Physiology 05.exp:
There are 5 primary taste sensations:

  1. Sweet

  2. Sour

  3. Salty

  4. Bitter

  5. Umami (savory)

High-yield Taste recall:
Five basic tastes = Sweet + Sour + Salty + Bitter + Umami.

Exam pearl:
“SSSBU” → Sweet, Sour, Salty, Bitter, Umami.

Physiology 05.question: ৩৫) Which sensation bypasses thalamus?
Physiology 05.exp:
Olfaction (smell) is the only major sensory modality that initially bypasses the thalamus. Olfactory receptor neurons project to the olfactory bulb → olfactory tract → primary olfactory cortex without a mandatory thalamic relay.

Other major sensory modalities have thalamic relay nuclei:

  • Vision → Lateral geniculate body (LGB)

  • Audition → Medial geniculate body (MGB)

  • Gustation → VPM nucleus of thalamus

High-yield Thalamus recall:
Olfaction → bypasses thalamus initially.
Vision → LGB
Audition → MGB
Taste → VPM

Exam pearl:
“All major senses relay through thalamus—except smell.”

Physiology 05.question: ৩৬) Which glial cell is mesodermal in origin?
Physiology 05.exp:
Microglia are the resident phagocytic immune cells of the CNS and are unique among CNS glial cells because they are derived from mesodermal/myeloid lineage.

The other glial cells are derived from neuroectoderm:

  • Astrocytes → neuroectoderm

  • Oligodendrocytes → neuroectoderm

  • Ependymal cells → neuroectoderm

High-yield Neuroglia recall:
Microglia → mesodermal (myeloid) origin
Astrocytes + oligodendrocytes + ependymal cells → neuroectodermal origin

Exam pearl:
“Microglia = macrophages of CNS = mesodermal origin.”

Physiology 05.question: ৩৭) Which neurotransmitter is both excitatory & inhibitory?
Physiology 05.exp:
5-HT (serotonin) can produce both excitatory and inhibitory effects, depending on the serotonin receptor subtype and the tissue/circuit involved.

  • GABA → predominantly inhibitory in the mature CNS

  • Glutamate → predominantly excitatory

  • Acetylcholine → generally excitatory at the neuromuscular junction, but can have inhibitory effects in some autonomic tissues

  • 5-HT → both excitatory and inhibitory effects

High-yield Neurotransmitter recall:
Glutamate → major excitatory neurotransmitter
GABA → major inhibitory neurotransmitter
5-HT → can be excitatory or inhibitory depending on receptor

Exam pearl:
“Serotonin can excite or inhibit—its effect depends on the receptor subtype.”

Physiology 05.question: ৩৮) Which lobe of brain is responsible for hearing?
Physiology 05.exp:
The primary auditory cortex is located in the superior temporal gyrus, specifically Heschl's (transverse temporal) gyri. It is responsible for the initial cortical processing of auditory information.

  • Frontal lobe → voluntary motor function, executive functions, speech production

  • Parietal lobe → somatosensory processing

  • Temporal lobe → hearing and auditory processing

  • Occipital lobe → vision

High-yield Cerebral cortex recall:
Temporal → hearing
Occipital → vision
Parietal → sensation
Frontal → motor function

Exam pearl:
“Hearing = Heschl's gyrus = Temporal lobe.”

Physiology 05.question: ৩৯) Which receptor is concerned with pressure & vibration?
Physiology 05.exp:
Pacinian (lamellar) corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors that detect deep pressure and high-frequency vibration. They are found mainly in the deep dermis/subcutaneous tissue and around joints and other deep tissues.

  • Free nerve endings → pain, temperature, crude touch

  • Pacinian corpuscles → deep pressure and vibration

  • Muscle spindle → muscle length/stretch

  • Golgi tendon organ → muscle tension

High-yield Sensory receptor recall:
Pacinian → pressure + vibration
Meissner → fine touch + low-frequency vibration
Muscle spindle → muscle length
Golgi tendon organ → muscle tension

Exam pearl:
“Pacinian = Pressure + Vibration.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪০) What is the structural & functional unit of nervous system?
Physiology 05.exp:
The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. It is specialized to receive, integrate, and transmit nerve impulses.

A typical neuron consists of:

  • Cell body (soma) → metabolic and integrative center

  • Dendrites → receive signals

  • Axon → conducts impulses away from the cell body

High-yield Nervous system recall:
Neuron = structural + functional unit of the nervous system.

Exam pearl:
“Neuron is the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪১) Retrograde degeneration occurs in which part of neuron?
Physiology 05.exp:
Retrograde degeneration occurs in the proximal segment of the axon after nerve injury and progresses toward the cell body. It may cause changes in the neuronal cell body, such as chromatolysis.

In contrast, Wallerian (anterograde) degeneration occurs in the distal segment of the axon, away from the cell body.

High-yield Nerve injury recall:

  • Retrograde degeneration → proximal axon → toward cell body

  • Wallerian degeneration → distal axon → away from cell body

  • Chromatolysis → cell body response to axonal injury

Exam pearl:
“Retrograde = toward the cell body; Wallerian = distal/away from the cell body.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪২) Which is the content of synaptic cleft?
Physiology 05.exp:
The synaptic cleft is the small extracellular space between the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes. At cholinergic synapses, acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is present in the synaptic cleft and rapidly hydrolyses acetylcholine into choline + acetate, terminating its action.

  • Calcium channels → presynaptic membrane

  • Acetylcholinesterase → synaptic cleft

  • Microtubules → axon/cytoplasm

  • cAMP → intracellular second messenger

High-yield Synapse recall:
ACh → AChE → choline + acetate
AChE is concentrated in the synaptic cleft/basal lamina at cholinergic synapses.

Exam pearl:
“Cholinergic synapse: AChE in the cleft terminates acetylcholine action.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪৩) The condition of eye with normal refractive power is called.....?
Physiology 05.exp:
Emmetropia is the condition in which the eye has normal refractive power, so parallel rays of light from a distant object are focused directly on the retina without accommodation.

  • Emmetropia → normal refraction

  • Ametropia → abnormal refraction

  • Myopia → focus in front of retina

  • Hypermetropia → focus behind retina

High-yield Eye optics recall:
Emmetropia = normal eye + image focused on retina.

Exam pearl:
“Normal refractive eye = Emmetropic eye.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪৪) What is the cause of Anisometropia?
Physiology 05.option1: Increase in anteroposterior diameter of the eyeball
Physiology 05.option2: Decrease in anteroposterior diameter of the eyeball
Physiology 05.option3: Difference in refractive power of both eyes
Physiology 05.exp:
Anisometropia is a condition in which the two eyes have unequal refractive power. This can result from differences in axial length, corneal curvature, or lens refractive power between the eyes.

  • Anisometropia → unequal refractive power between the two eyes

  • Increased anteroposterior diameter → myopia

  • Decreased anteroposterior diameter → hypermetropia

  • Loss of lens elasticity → presbyopia

High-yield Refractive error recall:
Anisometropia = unequal refraction between the two eyes → unequal retinal image size (aniseikonia) may occur.

Exam pearl:
“Aniso = unequal; anisometropia = unequal refractive power of the two eyes.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪৫) Which lens is used for correction of astigmatism?
Physiology 05.exp:
Astigmatism occurs when the cornea or lens has unequal curvature in different meridians, causing light rays to focus at different points. A cylindrical lens corrects this by providing refractive power in one meridian while having little or no power in the perpendicular meridian.

  • Biconcave lens → Myopia

  • Biconvex lens → Hypermetropia

  • Cylindrical lens → Astigmatism

  • Concave-convex → not the standard corrective lens for astigmatism

High-yield Refractive error recall:
Myopia → Concave lens
Hypermetropia → Convex lens
Astigmatism → Cylindrical lens
Presbyopia → Convex/reading lens

Exam pearl:
“Astigmatism = Cylindrical lens.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪৬) Which is a Causes for Nerve Deafness?
Physiology 05.exp:
Nerve (sensorineural) deafness occurs due to damage to the cochlea or auditory nerve. Streptomycin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic, is ototoxic and can damage the auditory apparatus, causing sensorineural hearing loss.

  • Otosclerosis → conductive deafness

  • Otitis media → usually conductive deafness

  • Streptomycin → sensorineural deafness (ototoxicity)

  • Foreign body in ear → conductive deafness

High-yield Hearing loss recall:
Conductive → external/middle ear pathology
Sensorineural → cochlea/auditory nerve pathology
Aminoglycosides → ototoxicity

Exam pearl:
“Streptomycin → ototoxic → sensorineural deafness.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪৭) Which nerve is not related to taste sensation?
Physiology 05.exp:
The trigeminal nerve (CN V) is not a special taste nerve. It carries general somatic sensation such as touch, pain, and temperature from the oral cavity, but not taste.

Taste is carried by:

  • Facial nerve (CN VII) → anterior 2/3 of tongue

  • Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) → posterior 1/3 of tongue

  • Vagus nerve (CN X) → epiglottis and lower pharyngeal region

High-yield Taste pathway recall:
Anterior 2/3 → CN VII (chorda tympani)
Posterior 1/3 → CN IX
Epiglottis → CN X

Exam pearl:
“V, VII, IX, X: V gives general sensation; VII, IX, X carry taste.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪৮) What is taste blindness?
Physiology 05.option2: Loss of ability to recognize substances by taste
Physiology 05.exp:
Taste blindness (ageusia) refers to the inability to perceive or recognize taste. In exam terminology, it is commonly described as a loss of the ability to recognize substances by taste.

  • Ageusia → complete loss of taste

  • Hypogeusia → decreased taste sensation

  • Dysgeusia → distorted/abnormal taste sensation

High-yield Taste disorders recall:
Ageusia = loss of taste
Hypogeusia = reduced taste
Dysgeusia = altered/distorted taste

Exam pearl:
“A = absent → Ageusia = absence/loss of taste.”

Physiology 05.question: ৪৯) Total loss of sensation of smell is called......?
Physiology 05.exp:
Anosmia means complete loss of the sense of smell due to dysfunction of the olfactory system.

  • Anosmia → complete loss of smell

  • Hyposmia → reduced sense of smell

  • Ageusia → complete loss of taste

  • Hypogeusia → reduced sense of taste

High-yield Olfactory disorders recall:
Anosmia = absent smell
Hyposmia = decreased smell
Parosmia = distorted smell perception

Exam pearl:
“An- = absence → Anosmia = total loss of smell.”

Physiology 05.question: ৫০) Which one is receptor for sweet taste?
Physiology 05.exp:
Sweet taste is detected by G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), specifically the T1R2/T1R3 heterodimer on taste receptor cells. Activation of these receptors triggers an intracellular second-messenger pathway leading to depolarization and neurotransmitter release.

  • Sweet → T1R2/T1R3 → GPCR

  • Umami → T1R1/T1R3 → GPCR

  • Bitter → T2R family → GPCR

  • Salty → ion channels such as ENaC

  • Sour → proton-sensitive mechanisms

High-yield Taste receptor recall:
Sweet, bitter, umami → GPCR-mediated
Salty and sour → primarily ion-channel/proton-mediated mechanisms

Exam pearl:
“Sweet = T1R2 + T1R3 = GPCR.”
